drills.q: Walk through the attention formula term by term.
drills.a: softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V: Q,K are linear projections of the input; QK^T scores query-key similarity; dividing by sqrt(d_k) controls variance so softmax doesn't saturate; softmax turns each row into a probability distribution over positions; multiplying by V produces a weighted average of value vectors.

drills.q: Derive why the scaling factor is sqrt(d_k) and not d_k.
drills.a: Dot product of d_k iid mean-0 unit-variance components has variance d_k (sum of d_k independent unit-variance products), so std dev grows as sqrt(d_k). Dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores unit variance regardless of d_k. Dividing by d_k over-shrinks variance below 1, pushing softmax toward uniform and destroying its ability to sharply prefer one key.

drills.q: What is the time and memory cost of naive self-attention, and which one actually limits you in practice?
drills.a: O(n^2*d_k) time, O(n^2) memory per head since QK^T is n x n. Memory is the practical limiter -- at n=8192 fp16 one head's score matrix alone is ~128MB, making naive attention infeasible at long context regardless of available compute.

drills.q: Compute the KV-cache reduction factor for Llama-family 70B (64 query heads, 8 KV heads via GQA) versus a hypothetical full-MHA config, and explain why pure MQA is rarely the right default.
drills.a: 8x reduction (h/g = 64/8). Pure MQA (1 shared KV head) would give a further 8x beyond that (64x vs MHA total) but measurably degrades summarization and long-context retrieval quality, since collapsing to one shared KV head removes representational diversity; GQA with a small group count recovers most of MHA's quality at most of the memory saving.

drills.q: Do the KV-cache arithmetic for a 70B model, 80 layers, GQA-8, head_dim=128, BF16, at 128k context, and explain the serving implication.
drills.a: 2*80*8*128*2 = 327,680 bytes/token = 0.32MB/token; at 128,000 tokens that's ~42GB for a SINGLE sequence -- larger than many GPUs' total VRAM. This means long-context serving is fundamentally a batching/admission-control problem, not just a bigger-GPU problem.

drills.q: Explain mechanically how MLA differs from GQA, and why the K up-projection can be folded into the query projection with no extra decode cost.
drills.a: MLA compresses K and V into a shared low-rank latent via a learned down-projection, caching only the latent and reconstructing per-head K/V via up-projection at attention time. Because both projections are linear, the K up-projection composes algebraically with the query projection, so it can be pre-merged into the query weights -- decode-time compute doesn't pay extra for reconstructing full-size K.

drills.q: A colleague claims FlashAttention is an approximation because it uses tiling. Correct them and explain why it's actually faster.
drills.a: Tiling changes memory access order, not the math -- FlashAttention computes the identical softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V via block processing and a running (online) softmax that rescales incrementally, which is algebraically exact. It's faster because the real bottleneck was HBM bandwidth (writing/reading the full n x n matrix), not FLOPs; keeping tiles in on-chip SRAM and only writing the final output cuts memory traffic dramatically even though FLOP count is essentially unchanged.

drills.q: Why does FlashAttention-3's speedup depend specifically on H100/Hopper hardware rather than being a pure algorithmic improvement portable to A100?
drills.a: FA3 exploits warp-specialized producer/consumer pipelining that overlaps Tensor Core matmuls with the asynchronous TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator), plus FP8 support with incoherent processing -- both are Hopper-generation hardware features absent on Ampere (A100). On A100 you'd fall back toward FA2-level gains, which come mainly from the shared tiling/IO-awareness idea rather than Hopper-specific async tricks.

drills.q: You're pretraining a new 30B model targeting 128k context on a fixed GPU memory budget. How do you approach the KV-head/latent design decision?
drills.a: Work backward from the KV-cache budget: decide max concurrent long-context sequences needed, compute bytes/token available after weights+activations, then choose n_kv_heads (GQA group count) or MLA latent rank to hit that number. Validate against long-context retrieval evals during architecture search, since an overly aggressive compression choice can't be cheaply fixed after pretraining -- it requires another training run, not a config change.

drills.q: A user reports the model "forgets" information from early in a very long conversation. Is this necessarily an attention-mechanism problem?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- full attention still computes exact scores over the whole context. More likely causes: the conversation exceeded the context window and got truncated, positional encoding degrading beyond trained lengths (a RoPE/ALiBi extrapolation issue), or serving-layer KV-cache eviction/quantization dropping those tokens' state. Diagnose by checking whether tokens are still in-window and whether the serving stack does any cache eviction before blaming attention itself.
